target_customer: Members of the Indian diaspora (NRIs) in the UK, US, Europe and UAE who send money home and need banking and investing across borders
problem: Cross-border money transfers and banking for migrants are costly, slow and fragmented, with poor exchange rates and no access to credit or investing in a new country.
business_model: Consumer fintech: remittance margin and FX spread, plus banking and investment product fees

founders.name: Parth Garg
previous_startups: Unnamed earlier company (YC page says second time founder)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch says he grew up in the UAE. Only founder listed on the YC page; no other co-founder confirmed in sources opened.

competitors.name: Wise (Transferwise)
competitors.what: Low cost international transfers and multi-currency accounts

competitors.name: Xflow
competitors.what: Cross-border payments product that Inc42 compared Vance features to

technical_complexity.rationale: Needed money movement rails, licensing partners and FX pricing across several corridors, which is standard fintech engineering with regulatory complexity rather than research.

defensibility.rationale: Remittance is a crowded category with low switching costs; licenses and diaspora focus give only modest protection.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Incumbents kept competing on price; TechCrunch in 2025 still named Remitly and Wise as global rivals and Abound as an India rival. No incumbent bought Aspora.

market_need_then: Large Indian diaspora remittance flows and high fees and FX spreads; Inc42 in October 2022 described the cross-border neobank gap. Company later reported remittance volume growing from 400 million to 2 billion dollars a year (TechCrunch, June 2025).

branding.name_origin: Aspora is derived from diaspora per company framing that the new name reflects people building lives across borders; one directory says the earlier name Vance was dropped in April 2025 because ads were flagged as political due to similarity with JD Vance. The company page does not state the political reason.
branding.domain_note: Now uses aspora.com; earlier domain history not found.

identity.visual_style: A brand agency case study (exactly.ai) credits a rebrand with local soul on a global scale
identity.voice_and_tone: Plain promises such as guaranteed Google rates

rebrands.why: Directory source says political ad flagging due to JD Vance similarity; company says new name better reflects its customers

brand_strength.rationale: Strong diaspora framing and a funded rebrand, but only a few years of exposure and limited independent press on the brand itself.

pivots.from: Pipe.com for India (non-dilutive capital for startups, per Inc42 at seed)
pivots.to: Remittances for NRIs in the UK, then Europe and UAE
pivots.why: TechCrunch says it began remittances in 2023 and expanded; reason not stated
Rebrand to a global diaspora identity

outcome_analysis: Aspora started as Vance, a YC W22 neobank idea, found traction in remittances for the Indian diaspora from 2023, and raised a 35 million dollar Series A and a roughly 50 million dollar Series B led by Sequoia with Greylock. Reported remittance volume grew sixfold in a year. It rebranded in 2025 and took control of a Lithuanian e-money firm in July 2026 to expand in Europe. It remains active with no sign of distress.
notes: Series B amount conflicts: TechCrunch says 50 million dollars, Entrepreneur India, Finextra and YourStory say 53 million; 53 million recorded. TechCrunch reports valuations of 150 million (Series A) and 500 million (Series B) but does not label them post-money, so post_money is null. Series A date inferred from last December in a June 2025 article; one source says December 2023. Headquarters reported as London by some sources and Belfast by another. Total raised quoted as 93 or 99 million.
